title: Las Animas County CO well depth and cost
meta_description: Median well depth 150 ft and median yield 6.5 gpm in Las Animas County, Colorado; see drilling cost, water levels, trends and buyer tips.
h1: Water wells in Las Animas County, Colorado
intro_html: Las Animas County covers a lot of ground, from the Trinidad area out across the plains, and the well logs show almost every kind of outcome. Depths range from very shallow to more than 2,000 feet, and yields are usually serviceable but not huge. If you’re looking at land here, it pays to understand what nearby wells are actually doing before you commit to a build or a purchase.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Las Animas County
sections.html:
Across Las Animas County, wells with a reported depth have a median of about 150 feet. The middle half fall between 70 and 300 feet, so a driller’s “typical” bid will usually be based on something in that range. About 33% of wells are under 100 feet, another 40% are 100–300 feet, and 19% go 300–600 feet. A smaller group, about 7%, are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest well on record runs down to 2,458 feet.

On these plains and sedimentary rocks, depth is driven by local geology and which fractured-bedrock zone your driller can hit. Most permits list an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with a few in the Dakota and Cheyenne aquifers. Plan for the common 70–300 foot outcome, but leave budget room in case your site falls into one of the deeper pockets.

sections.heading: Water table and what it’s doing over time
sections.html:
Static water levels reported in the county have a median of about 54 feet below ground, with the middle half between 30 and 178 feet. That means many wells have a fair column of water above the pump, but some areas put water quite a bit deeper. Looking by decade, median levels were about 51 feet in the 2000s, dropped to around 100 feet in the 2010s, then improved to about 45 feet in the 2020s.

That pattern suggests local ups and downs rather than a simple long-term decline. In one pocket you might see shallower water in newer wells; a few miles away, it could be the opposite. Before buying, pull records for the closest constructed wells near places like Trinidad, Aguilar, or Kim and compare their water levels and dates.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water to expect here
sections.html:
For wells that report a pump test, the median yield in Las Animas County is about 6.5 gallons per minute. The middle half of wells produce between 3.0 and 10.0 gpm. That’s enough for a typical exempt household well and some outdoor use if you manage it, but it’s not high-production irrigation water.

Only about 3% of wells come in under 1 gpm, which are the marginal or problem wells a buyer worries about. Roughly 28% land between 1 and 5 gpm, 58% fall in the 5–15 gpm band, and about 11% exceed 15 gpm. The fractured-bedrock setting means yields can vary sharply over short distances, so the single best predictor for your lot is how nearby wells in the same geologic zone are performing.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit trends
sections.html:
Las Animas County has 7,988 wells in the state records, with 5,785 shown as constructed and 3,088 listing a total depth. Permitting really picked up in recent decades: 356 wells in the 1970s, 350 in the 1980s, 1,171 in the 1990s, 845 in the 2000s, and a big jump to 3,660 in the 2010s. There are already 341 permits in the 2020s, and the newest permit is from 2025.

Most uses are split between domestic or household wells at about 34% and stock wells at around 26%, with some monitoring and a small amount of irrigation. The records show Boday Well Drilling (Alex and Kathleen Boday) and Snyder Well Pump Service as the most active drillers here, which tells you there’s an established group of contractors familiar with local conditions.

sections.heading: What a new well typically costs in Las Animas County
sections.html:
Here the ground is mainly alluvium and plains sedimentary rock, and current drilling runs about $35–$55 per foot. At the county’s 150-foot median depth, that puts the borehole itself in the ballpark of $5,200–$8,200. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that depth usually totals around $11,200–$20,200.

If you end up in one of the deeper 300–600 foot zones, the per-foot cost stacks up quickly. When budgeting for raw land, I’d model a 300-foot well at your site-specific rate, then be pleasantly surprised if you hit water closer to the 150-foot median.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, contamination, and building layout
sections.html:
Low yield is the main well risk here, even though only about 3% of tested wells report under 1 gpm. A thin or fractured-bedrock zone can mean lots of depth with not much water. With 703 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 304 historic mine features, and one EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles in the county, you should also pay attention to water quality and siting.

Plan your septic and well layout early so you maintain required separations and keep them uphill of any old mine workings or drainage if possible. For a new build, budget for lab testing of a new well and consider filtration if you’re down-gradient of industrial or transportation corridors.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Las Animas County
sections.html:
Before you make an offer, pull the Colorado DWR well records around your parcel in places like Trinidad, Aguilar, Kim, or the surrounding plains. Look closely at reported depths, yields, and static water levels, not just the closest well but several within the same drainage or geologic setting.

Ask if an existing well is permitted for the use you need; many here are domestic or stock, and changing use can require new permitting or augmentation in tighter basins. On vacant land, tie your purchase contract to a successful well with a minimum yield based on your plans. Then line up a local driller who knows the fractured-bedrock character of this county and can explain what they’re seeing as they go down.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Las Animas County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Las Animas County, wells that report a depth have a median of about 150 feet. The middle half fall between 70 and 300 feet, so many are relatively shallow to moderate. About 33% of wells are under 100 feet, while 19% run 300–600 feet and about 7% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest well on record at 2,458 feet.

faq.q: What is a good well yield in Las Animas County, CO?
faq.a: Reported wells in Las Animas County have a median yield of about 6.5 gpm, with most between 3.0 and 10.0 gpm. Only about 3% of tested wells are under 1 gpm, which are the ones that can be problematic. Around 58% produce 5–15 gpm, which is generally adequate for a household well if you manage outdoor use and storage sensibly.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Las Animas County?
faq.a: Drilling here typically runs about $35–$55 per foot in the local alluvium and sedimentary rock. At the county’s 150-foot median depth, the borehole alone is roughly $5,200–$8,200. Once you add casing, pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, a complete domestic well at that depth usually ends up around $11,200–$20,200, with deeper wells costing proportionally more.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Las Animas County?
faq.a: The limited static water level data don’t show a simple steady decline. Median depth to water was about 51 feet in the 2000s, deeper at around 100 feet in the 2010s, then shallower at roughly 45 feet in the 2020s. That points to local and time-based variation. The best way to judge your area is to compare levels and dates from several nearby wells in the DWR records.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Las Animas County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The county has 703 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 304 historic mine features, and one EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles, so quality can vary by location. Many domestic wells are used for household supply, but you should always have a new or existing well lab-tested and consider treatment if you’re near industrial areas, mines, or major highways.
